extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato/classical philosophy; those studying poetry, imitation, and censorship in the Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Plato's standards for poetry and imitation as presented in Book X of the Republic — including his arguments for exclusion/censorship, the epistemic dangers of poetic imitation, and the role of literature in education and moral psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation about poetry / exclusion of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Many things pleased me in the order of our State, but there was nothing which I liked better than the regulation about poetry.’ — Plato argues for excluding imitation from the well-ordered State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato treats poetry as potentially harmful to understanding and the polity: he defends regulating or excluding poetic imitation on political and educational grounds. The commentary connects the regulation to the division of the soul and the danger that imitation poses to those lacking philosophical knowledge. This rubric is justified by the claim that imitation fosters false images and errors in the many, and so should be restricted in a city that aims to cultivate the better principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is an outrage on the understanding unless corrected
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘All poetry is an outrage on the understanding, unless the hearers have that balm of knowledge which heals error.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's standard for when poetry is permissible: only when an audience possesses sufficient philosophical knowledge to correct the false impressions poetry creates. The passage implies an evaluative test for any poetic work: would it mislead an unphilosophical audience into error? If yes, it is objectionable; if the audience can 'heal' the error with knowledge, the work is less dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as thrice-removed from truth (the maker/carpenter/painter example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The maker (God) makes the Form/true bed; the carpenter makes the bed according to the Form; the painter imitates the carpenter’s bed — the poet/painter is thrice removed from the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's ontology of representation is an evaluative criterion: artistic imitation is a copy of a copy and therefore epistemically inferior. The text uses the bed/carpenter/painter example to show that the tragic poet is 'thrice removed from the king and from the truth' and hence liable to deceive. Works that are only images of appearances are to be judged as low epistemic value and potentially corrupting, especially for the uninstructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets produce deceptive images that mislead the simple
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He can paint any other artist, although he knows nothing of their arts; and this with sufficient skill to deceive children or simple people.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical evaluative point: assess whether a poetic or pictorial work deceives those without technical or philosophical knowledge — i.e., whether it gives a plausible but shallow simulacrum that misinforms. The passage warns that skillful imitation can persuade and mislead the uninstructed, an anti-pattern to be checked when approving or teaching works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature should promote the pleasures of reason rather than sensual pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato distinguishes three kinds of pleasure (reason, passion, desire) and holds that the pleasures of reason are 'truer' and more proper to a good life than sensual or beastly pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating literature, ask which part of the soul its pleasures address: does it cultivate intellectual/rational pleasure (worthy, stable), or does it appeal primarily to bodily/sensual and passion-driven pleasures (transient, illusive)? Plato’s ideal literary aim is to foster rational pleasures and the 'true upper' satisfactions rather than merely animate lower appetites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of literature in education: strengthen the better principle / self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The intention in educating the young, is to give them self-control; the law desires to nurse up in them a higher principle...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplies an educational criterion for approving works: literature should be judged by whether it helps cultivate self-control and the 'better principle' in the young. Works that exacerbate the 'beastly' elements or habituate spirited parts to base desires (flattery, effeminacy, luxury) fail this test and should be restricted or reformed in pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about poetic/tragic imitation in moral formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic poets and imitators are implicated in forming character; their images may strengthen or weaken parts of the soul (lion, serpent, many-headed beast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the moral effects of poetic representation on character: whether a work encourages temperance, courage, justice, and wisdom, or whether it trains children and citizens in vice (flattery, effeminacy, lust, lawlessness). The commentary repeatedly ties artistic content to its formative moral outcomes, urging scrutiny of artistic influence on habits and desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allegory, number, and musical harmony as symbolic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato uses numerical/harmonic symbols (e.g., the Pythagorean triangle, 3–4–5; the number 216; the interval 729) and musical ratios (4/3) to signify moral, political, or psychological relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an artistic technique, symbolic/arithmetic allegory is presented as a legitimate vehicle for expressing moral and political truths. The commentary notes both the suggestive force and the fancifulness of such numerological metaphors: they can illuminate relations (e.g., measuring the interval between king and tyrant), but one should beware of mistaking formal arithmetic manipulation for substantive proof. Use symbolic devices to illuminate, not to substitute for argument.
